title: The Charge That Changes the Odds

scenes.tts: How can a small mark change what a protein does without rebuilding it? Watch this population of protein copies. Each copy flickers among shapes, and those shapes make different contacts. The cell will change the odds, not manufacture a replacement. That is faster than waiting to make new protein.

Fill the frame with a population of rounded protein blocks continuously flexing between two schematic shapes. A grey factory assembling a replacement stays far in the background while a gold question mark tracks an existing protein.

scenes.visual: The carried protein population shrinks behind the title 'The Charge That Changes the Odds'. Keep the teal proteins gently flexing so the frame never freezes.

scenes.tts: A kinase brings A T P beside a hydroxyl-bearing site on a protein. The kinase transfers the end phosphate, leaving A D P. In animal signaling, the best-studied targets are serine, threonine, and tyrosine. The protein remains the same chain, but its local chemistry has changed. This attachment is a reversible covalent modification.

scenes.visual: Zoom into one teal protein block. A blue kinase carries a violet ATP chip to a labelled hydroxyl site. The terminal gold phosphate transfers; the ATP chip becomes ADP. Serine, threonine and tyrosine labels orbit the site without molecular structures. The protein outline remains continuous.

scenes.tts: Near neutral P H, the attached phosphate carries a strong negative charge. Put that charge among the protein's other charges. Attractions strengthen in some arrangements and weaken in others. The population shifts toward shapes and contacts that accommodate the new charge. Partners can also read the phosphate's shape. Phosphate changes probabilities; it does not issue a universal command.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction choices while the central phosphorylated protein continues a slow flex. Do not reveal or highlight any choice.

scenes.tts: Phosphorylation shifts glycogen phosphorylase toward activity. It inhibits glycogen synthase, which builds glycogen. The direction depends on the protein and the site. The same charge can favor a different shape or disrupt a different contact.

scenes.visual: Split the carried population into two labelled schematic groups. Gold phosphate shifts the glycogen phosphorylase tally toward 'active' but shifts the glycogen synthase tally toward 'inhibited'. Never show every copy in one state. Replace the three choices with 'depends on target'.

scenes.tts: Sometimes the important change is a contact, not catalytic activity. A partner can recognize the phosphorylated surface and dock. Elsewhere, the mark can expose or hide a location signal. A phosphate can also prepare a nearby site for another kinase. These are different outcomes of the same physical change.

scenes.visual: Transform one teal protein through three connected schematic motions. First a pocketed partner closes around the gold badge. Then a location tag slides from covered to exposed. Finally a second blue kinase approaches a nearby blank site after the first badge appears. Label the sequence 'docking', 'location', 'priming'.

scenes.tts: The mark lasts until an enzyme removes it. A phosphatase uses water to release inorganic phosphate and restore the unmodified site. It does not reverse the kinase reaction or remake A T P. Writing and erasing are separate reactions, controlled by separate enzymes. A complete trip spends an A T P molecule.
scenes.caption: The mark lasts until an enzyme removes it. A phosphatase uses water to release inorganic phosphate and restore the unmodified site. It does not reverse the kinase reaction or remake ATP. Writing and erasing are separate reactions, controlled by separate enzymes. A complete trip spends an ATP molecule.
scenes.visual: Carry the phosphorylated teal protein into a lower lane. A red phosphatase and water chip remove the gold badge, which leaves as inorganic phosphate. Above, the blue kinase lane remains separate. Cross out a reversed kinase arrow. One ATP counter on screen decreases by one for the completed loop.

scenes.tts: That separation makes the mark both stable and reversible. A T P is plentiful enough that a kinase rarely waits for its donor. The phosphate persists without an eraser, yet can disappear quickly when a phosphatase acts. Cells can therefore alter existing proteins faster than rebuilding the whole population.

scenes.visual: Return to the full teal population. Gold badges remain fixed while the red phosphatase is absent. Bring the phosphatase back and sweep badges away in a wave. Violet ATP chips drift near the blue kinase. The distant grey protein factory remains slower and dimmer.

scenes.tts: Carry this rule into every case. Ask where the phosphate appears, which shapes or partners it favors, and what removal restores. The outcome may be activity, inhibition, docking, movement, or priming. The common cause is a stable phosphate, read through its charge and shape, that an enzyme can erase.
